A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Draft:

Who Should Design the Summer Project?

Every June, a packet goes home in my cousin's backpack. It has a reading list of three novels, a worksheet for each one, and a rubric stapled to the back. Every August, the night before school starts, he fills in the worksheets at the kitchen table using chapter summaries he found online. He gets full credit. He has not learned anything, except maybe how fast he can write when he is panicking. I think his school has the right goal and the wrong method. Summer projects should be designed by students, with teachers setting the limits and checking the plan.

The main reason is simple: people work harder on things they chose. During the school year, a student can be pushed through an assignment he does not care about because the teacher is standing there five days a week. In the summer nobody is standing there. The only thing that keeps a project going through July is the student's own interest. A girl who loves baking and decides to test how different amounts of baking soda change a cookie is going to run that experiment six or seven times, because she wants to eat the results and because she is honestly curious which batch will come out flat. She will measure, record, compare, and write up what happened. That is the scientific method, and no one had to force it. Give the same girl a packet on the phases of the moon and she will do exactly what my cousin does.

A second reason is that designing the project is itself a skill worth learning. When a teacher hands over a finished assignment, all the hardest thinking has already been done: choosing a question, deciding what counts as an answer, figuring out how long each part will take. Students almost never get to practice those steps, and then they arrive at college or a job and are expected to know them. A student who plans to interview her grandfather about leaving Vietnam has to decide what to ask, how to record it, and what to do when he does not want to talk about a certain year. A student who wants to build a birdhouse has to price the wood and realize he measured wrong. Those problems are frustrating, and they teach more than a rubric does.

Third, summers are not equal. A teacher-designed project assumes every student has the same summer, and they do not. One student is at a lake for two months. Another is watching her little brothers every day while her parents work. Another has a job at a grocery store. A project that requires visiting a museum or using a fast internet connection is easy for some and nearly impossible for others. When students design their own, they can build around the life they actually have. The girl babysitting her brothers can study how a four-year-old learns to read by teaching one. The boy at the grocery store can track prices for ten weeks and graph them.

The strongest argument on the other side is that some students will pick something too easy, or will pick nothing. That is a real problem, and it is why I do not think teachers should disappear from the process. Before school lets out, each student should turn in a one-page proposal: the question, the plan, and what the final product will be. The teacher approves it or sends it back with comments. The teacher can also require that every project include some reading, some writing, and some kind of evidence. That way the standards stay the teacher's, but the subject belongs to the student. A teacher who reads thirty proposals in June will also read thirty different projects in September instead of thirty copies of the same worksheet, which has to be more interesting for her too.

The purpose of a summer project is to keep students learning when no one is making them. A packet cannot do that. A question the student actually wants answered can.
